intro.text: Almost nothing on the SR-71 came off the shelf: not the fuel, the engines, the metal, the navigation or the suits its crews wore. It was designed to cruise at Mach 3.2 and cleared to 85,000 feet. These are its systems, as the flight manual the Air Force flew it by and the NASA reports written about it describe them.

sections.title: The inlet did most of the work

paras.text: At cruise the J58 was not the main source of thrust. A Lockheed breakdown quoted by NASA historian Peter Merlin gives the inlet 54 percent of the thrust at Mach 3, the ejector nozzle behind the engine 29 percent and the engine itself 17 percent. At Mach 2.2 the engine still supplied 73 percent. NASA's own fact sheet puts it plainly: less than 20 percent of the thrust at Mach 3 came from the engine.

Each inlet is a mixed-compression design with a spike that moves. The spike is locked forward on the ground and below 30,000 feet. From Mach 1.6 it moves aft about 1-5/8 inches for every 0.1 Mach, to about 26 inches. As it retracts, the throat closes to 54 percent of its Mach 1.6 area while the air the inlet captures more than doubles.

Two rings of doors keep the shock wave where it belongs. Forward bypass doors just behind the throat spill air overboard to hold the shock at the throat; aft bypass doors just ahead of the engine send air around it to the ejector. If the shock is thrown out of the inlet, an unstart, a sensor sees compressor inlet pressure fall by more than 23 percent, opens the forward bypass fully and drives the spike forward by up to 15 inches, then retracts it 3.75 seconds later.

NASA's YF-12 flights measured how fast an unstart happens: the shock reached the spike tip in about a hundredth of a second. Between Mach 2.3 and 2.6 an unstart was violent enough to snap a pilot's head and helmet against the inside of the canopy.

sections.title: The J58, built to burn in afterburner for hours

paras.text: Two Pratt & Whitney J58s, company designation JT11D-20, each rated at 34,000 lb of thrust in maximum afterburner at sea level. The 32,500 lb often quoted belongs to the early engine with fixed inlet guide vanes; the A-12's version was rated at 31,500 lb.

Its compressor has nine stages and a pressure ratio of only 8.8 to 1, because at cruise the inlet does most of the compressing. From about Mach 1.8 to 2.0, air bled from the fourth stage flows through six tubes around the rest of the engine and straight into the afterburner.
It was designed for Mach 3.2 with both full military power and afterburner run continuously, and its own fuel served as the hydraulic fluid for the nozzle, guide vanes and bleeds, at up to 1,800 psi.

The CIA's history says JP-7 is so hard to light that a lit match will not ignite it; no test of that is on record. Either way, the engines are lit chemically, with triethylborane, which burns on contact with air. Each engine carries enough for at least 16 shots, and a counter beside each throttle counts them down.
Turning a J58 over to start took more than 600 horsepower. Lockheed's answer was a cart carrying two Buick racing car engines, geared together to the engine's starter drive.

sections.title: Two cockpits, and only one has a stick

paras.text: The pilot's centre panel alone has 50 numbered items in the flight manual. The attitude director indicator sits in the middle. The inlet controls are grouped at the lower left: spike and forward bypass knobs graduated in Mach from 1.4 to 3.2, and a spike position indicator reading 0 to 26 inches. The engine instruments run down the right: tachometers, exhaust gas temperature, nozzle position, fuel flow and oil pressure.
A triple display indicator shows speed, altitude and Mach in digits. Its altitude window reads to 99,950 feet and drops the first digit above 100,000.

Behind the pilot sits the reconnaissance systems officer, who has no flight controls: a downward-looking viewsight at the top of the panel, a radar display below it, and the sensor and navigation panels on the consoles.

The astro-inertial navigation system steers by the stars, day and night. A telescope behind the rear cockpit looks up through a window and tracks stars from a 61-star catalogue; in astro-inertial mode the expected position error is 0.3 nautical miles for up to 10 hours.
At cruise the skin averaged 462 to 622 °F and reached 1,050 °F on the nacelles. Titanium alloys make up 93 percent of the structural weight.

The wing skins are corrugated chordwise so they can expand without buckling. Kelly Johnson wrote that at design heating the corrugations merely deepened by a few thousandths of an inch. The airframe as a whole grows by up to four inches in length.
It is painted black to radiate heat away. In the cockpit the outer glass reached 420 °F while the cooling air came in at minus 40 °F.

sections.title: Fuel as coolant, nitrogen as insurance

paras.text: Eight tanks hold 12,219 US gallons, 80,280 lb of JP-7. Before it is burned, the fuel cools the air conditioning, the hydraulic fluid and the engine oil; once it passes 290 °F, the hottest fuel is sent back to tank 4 instead of to the engines.
Liquid nitrogen, 262 liters in three flasks, pressurises the tanks and fills the space above the hot fuel so it cannot ignite. Without it the aircraft is limited to Mach 2.6.
In the air it took on fuel at about 6,000 lb a minute, every tank filling at once in 12 to 15 minutes, from a dedicated fleet of KC-135Q tankers.

Both crew sat on Lockheed SR-1 rocket ejection seats, usable from zero speed and altitude to the edge of the flight envelope. Pulling the D-ring jettisons the canopy and then fires the catapult; the rocket lights as the seat clears the sills, a drogue opens from the headrest, and at 15,000 feet the seat throws its occupant clear before a 35-foot parachute opens.
From late 1978 until 1996 they flew in David Clark S1030 full-pressure suits: six layers that hold 3.5 psi if the cockpit loses pressure.

states.forward_bypass: Open as required to place the shock

model.text: Article 121 built this model in Blender from NASA Dryden's vector three-view of the SR-71A, put on true scale with the fuselage stations in a NASA wind-tunnel report (nose at station 102, tail cone at 1355). The cross-sections are measured from a Lockheed lines drawing whose original has not yet been traced to a government archive; the inlet and spike come from Lockheed's YF-12 inlet report, and the nacelle exit, the chine to wing junction and the panel lines from the flight manual and NASA's YF-12 structure report. It is a reconstruction, not a scan: the engine internals, cockpits and markings are representative.

nose-section.title: Nose section
nose-section.text: The nose ahead of the cockpits could be exchanged. SR-71s flew with chined noses carrying the CAPRE side-looking radar, the optical bar camera or the ASARS radar; the ASARS nose had a one-piece quartz and polyimide radome-chine.

pitot-probe.title: Pitot-static probe
pitot-probe.text: The pitot-static boom on the nose tip, as drawn on NASA's three-view.

forward-fuselage.title: Forward fuselage and cockpits
forward-fuselage.text: Two cockpits in tandem, the pilot forward and the reconnaissance systems officer behind, each under its own canopy. The cockpits held a 26,000 ft or 10,000 ft pressure schedule. The red RESCUE arrows and ejection seat triangles are the A-12 ground handling manual's crash rescue markings, drawn from its figure; their places on the SR-71A and their colour are placeholders, since the manual gives neither.

canopy-glass.title: Windshield and canopy glass
canopy-glass.text: At cruise the outer glass reached 420 °F while the crew's cooling air came in at minus 40 °F.

chine-forebody.title: Chine forebody
chine-forebody.text: The chines run from the nose to the wing and carried almost 20 percent of the lift. The bays inside them carried sensors and equipment, listed on the flight manual's bay locator.

centre-body.title: Centre body and fuel
centre-body.text: The centre body carries the wing through and holds most of the fuel: eight tanks, 80,280 lb of JP-7. The fuel cooled the cockpit air, the hydraulics and the engine oil before it was burned.

tail-cone.title: Tail cone
tail-cone.text: The fuselage ends in a tail cone behind the wing. Like the chines, wing edges, spike cones and fins, it used heat-resistant non-metallic laminates in places.

inner-wing-l.title: Inner wing
inner-wing-l.text: A multispar, multirib wing whose skins are corrugated chordwise so they can grow with heat without buckling; at design heating the corrugations deepened by only a few thousandths of an inch. Inboard elevons on the trailing edge.

outer-wing-l.text: Outboard of the nacelles the leading edge droops in conical camber. The outboard elevons, each moved by 14 actuating cylinders, give pitch and roll control.

fin-l.text: All-moving rudders on fixed stub fins on top of the nacelles, each canted inward 15 degrees, driven by dual A and B hydraulic servos.

fuselage-frames.title: Fuselage frames
fuselage-frames.text: Frames at the bulkheads the flight manual shows (the nose joint, the cockpit bulkheads, the tank ends) and the wing beams carried across the fuselage on a 16 in pitch. The SR-71A's own frame stations are not public; these follow NASA's YF-12A structure drawing, which shares the SR-71's stations from the wing aft, and the flight manual figures.

longerons.title: Longerons
longerons.text: The forebody is a ring-stiffened cylinder with longerons at the top, bottom and sides; bending is carried mainly by the longerons on the top and bottom centrelines.

wing-structure.title: Wing beams and ribs
wing-structure.text: Spanwise beams on a 16 in pitch, and ribs at wing stations 72, 100 and 127 in the inner box and 213, 241 and 267 in the outer panel, from NASA's labelled YF-12A structure drawings. The skins between them are corrugated chordwise so they can grow with heat.

tank-1a.title: Tank 1A
tank-1a.text: A small tank immediately forward of tank 1 and feeding it, under the air refuelling receptacle: 251 US gal, 1,650 lb of JP-7. Stations are scaled from the flight manual's tank drawing, to about plus or minus 25 in.

tank-1.title: Tank 1
tank-1.text: 2,096 US gal, 13,770 lb of JP-7, with four boost pumps and the nitrogen heat exchanger. Stations are scaled from the flight manual's tank drawing, to about plus or minus 25 in.

tank-2.title: Tank 2

panel-pilot.title: Pilot's instrument panel
panel-pilot.text: The flight manual's drawing of the panel, on the panel: 50 numbered items, from the attitude director indicator in the middle to the inlet controls at lower left. See the panel explorer below.

panel-rso.text: The flight manual's drawing of the reconnaissance systems officer's panel, on the panel: viewsight at the top, radar display below, no flight controls.

bay-a.title: Compartment A, nose
bay-a.text: Radar or optical bar camera equipment in the interchangeable nose.

bay-b.title: Compartment B, left chine
bay-b.text: The left forward chine bay: the third liquid nitrogen Dewar and the pressure transducer assembly.

bay-d.title: Compartment D, right chine
bay-d.text: The right chine bay, carrying defensive electronics (DEF A2, C2 and M).

bay-km.title: Left forward mission bay (K, M)
bay-km.text: Compartment K, forward, with the DEF H system; compartment M, aft, with the digital and EIP recorders.

bay-ln.title: Right forward mission bay (L, N)
bay-ln.text: Compartments L and N, carrying radar recorders.

bay-ps.title: Left aft mission bay (P, S)
bay-ps.text: Compartment P, forward, with a technical objective camera; compartment S, aft, with the EIP electronic intelligence equipment.

bay-qt.title: Right aft mission bay (Q, T)
bay-qt.text: Compartment Q, forward, with a technical objective camera or radar recorder; compartment T, aft, with EIP equipment.

bay-ans.title: Astro-inertial navigation bay
bay-ans.text: The guidance group (inertial platform, star-tracking telescope and computer) is mounted in the fuselage aft of the rear cockpit, beside the air conditioning bay.

star-tracker.title: Star tracker window
star-tracker.text: The ANS telescope looks up through this window in a 78 degree cone, its axis vertical when the nose is 7.5 degrees up, tracking stars by day and night.

ar-receptacle.title: Air refuelling receptacle
ar-receptacle.text: On the spine above tank 1A. The flight manual's figure shows the door without a label; its identification here is inferred from the tank drawing. Tankers delivered about 6,000 lb a minute.

drag-chute.title: Drag chute compartment
drag-chute.text: Above tank 4: a 42 in pilot chute, a 10 ft extraction chute and a 40 ft ribbon drag chute, deployed at up to 210 KIAS.

main-gear.title: Main landing gear
main-gear.text: Three-wheel bogies that retract inboard into the fuselage, between tanks 3 and 4. Shown stowed; wheel size from the flight manual, layout representative.

j58-nozzle-r.text: The engine's own variable-area nozzle, moved by four actuators using engine fuel as hydraulic fluid; the cockpit gauge reads 0 (closed) to 10 (open). The airframe's ejector nozzle surrounds it.

j58-gearbox.title: Gearbox and accessories
j58-gearbox.text: The main gearbox at the bottom of the engine, with the main fuel pump and fuel control. Ground starts turned a starter gear on this gearbox from an external cart. The small tank on the side stands for the TEB tank.

cockpit.title: Cockpit
cockpit.text: The sealed crew compartment: the pilot's cockpit from the instrument panel at about station 258 to the bulkhead at 316, the reconnaissance systems officer's from about 318 to 382. The tub shape here is representative.

note.text: Marked in one-inch steps from 0, fully forward, to 26, fully aft.
Two pointers, left and right inlet, in percent open.
Left and right needles plus a striped needle showing the pressure DAFICS expects. Left and right should not differ by more than 1 psi.
A T-handle: pull to deploy the drag chute; rotate left and pull for emergency deployment.

items.name: Air Refuel Ready - Disc Pushbutton and Light

note.text: A 3-inch instrument at the top centre. The inset shows the 2-inch unit fitted without service bulletin R-2466.
The attitude director indicator, the largest instrument on the panel.
Mounted in the canopy, not on the panel.
Main dial to 10,000 rpm with a 1,000 rpm subdial. The tachometers power themselves.
Digital, reading 0 to 1,198 °C, with a red warning light at 860 °C. At cruise the engines ran at 775 to 805 °C.
Dial in 5,000 lb per hour steps to 95,000 lb per hour, with a five-digit window.

items.name: L and R Hydraulic Systems Pressure Gage

note.text: Pressure in the L and R hydraulic systems, which move the inlet spikes and bypass doors.

items.name: A and B Hydraulic Systems Pressure Gage

note.text: Pressure in the A and B hydraulic systems, which move the flight control surfaces.
Speed (KEAS), altitude and Mach in digits, computed by DAFICS. The altitude window reads to 99,950 ft and drops the first digit above 100,000 ft.
Left and right knobs: AUTO, OPEN, and a manual schedule.
Left and right knobs with AUTO, FWD and a manual scale graduated in Mach from 1.4 to 3.2.
Left and right toggles that restart an inlet after an unstart.
